criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community domestic water service access alongside agricultural and other uses in the Kirindi Oya system, specifically piped domestic water supply distributed via community standposts (15-20 households per standpost) by the National Water Supply and Drainage Board (NWS&DB), wells, and dry-season domestic canal water releases.
criterion_notes.c2: Both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading are satisfied (plain=yes, narrow=yes). Under the plain reading, the study examines formal water rights, institutional mandates, Farmers' Organizations, Standpipe Committees, and the Project Management Committee. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly analyzes concrete rules governing household domestic water access: NWS&DB permitted-use rules restricting standpipe water exclusively to drinking and prohibiting piped water use for homestead gardens; tariff/cost-recovery and enforcement rules requiring informal standpipe committees to collect Rs 11/month per household and imposing water disconnection plus a Rs 250 reconnection fee for misuse; local user discretion/accommodation tolerating bathing, clothes washing, pilgrim use, and small-enterprise use when alternatives are lacking; reservoir drought priority rules for domestic supply; and formal membership/eligibility rules excluding non-cultivators, women's domestic water interests, NWS&DB, and Standpipe Committees from system-level allocation bodies.
criterion_notes.c3: Mixed-methods socio-legal empirical case study based on field research including a stratified household survey (78 households in the old area and 78 households in the new area; N=156), water quality testing, direct observations at standpipes and tanks, about 10 focus group discussions, and key informant interviews with NWS&DB, Irrigation Department officials, and Standpipe Committees. Qualitative/mixed-methods socio-legal studies are eligible for the mechanism synthesis without a quantitative effect size.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative and descriptive empirical outcomes on household domestic water access and source reliance (piped standposts vs. wells and 14-day dry-season canal releases), low service reliability and continuity at standpipes (supplied only a few hours per day at varying times), disconnection/reconnection enforcement, de facto accommodated access for non-drinking domestic uses, and institutional exclusion from seasonal allocation decisions.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (households, 15-20 household standpipe user groups, and system governance bodies in Kirindi Oya, Sri Lanka; N=156 surveyed households plus focus groups, observations, and key informant interviews), rule-type exposures, domestic access/reliability outcomes, and mixed-methods case study design are clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: Further direct observations at standpipes and tanks were done and about 10 focus group discussions with, among others, women cultivators and curd pot makers.
Women, who may have stronger interests in domestic water supply or other uses, are not directly involved. Formal water rights are recognized only for irrigation and domestic water.
There is no recognized water right for homestead gardens. To the contrary, taking water from either the irrigation canals or piped water supply for gardens is formally prohibited.

15 to 20 households make use of the same standpost. These standpipe committees are informal, i.e., no authority is vested in them, although they are responsible for collecting user charges of Rs 11 per month from the households who make use of the standposts.

Those rules and regulations specify that water from the standpipes can only be used for drinking purposes. However, during key informant interviews and focus group discussions, other uses like bathing, business use, and washing clothes were reported.
Reliability of water supply through standpipes is quite low. Water is supplied for only a few hours a day and these hours can vary every day.

raw_response.exposure: Formal and informal water rights and rule-type governance mechanisms: NWS&DB standpipe permitted-use rules (drinking-only restriction and prohibition on garden watering), monthly household user charges (Rs 11/month), collective liability with disconnection and Rs 250 reconnection fee enforcement, informal standpipe user discretion/accommodation of non-drinking uses, drought priority allocation rules, and membership/representation rules of Farmers' Organizations and the Project Management Committee.
raw_response.outcome: Household and community domestic water access across piped standposts, wells, and dry-season canal releases; standpipe service reliability and continuity (low reliability, a few variable hours per day); de facto accommodated access for bathing, washing, and small enterprises; and exclusion of domestic water users and women from formal system-level allocation decisions.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Inhabitants (~87,750 across old and new irrigated areas) and water user groups (including standpipe groups of 15-20 households) in the Kirindi Oya irrigation system, southeastern Sri Lanka; stratified survey of 156 households (78 in old area, 78 in new area), ~10 focus group discussions, direct observations at standpipes and tanks, and key informant interviews.
raw_response.rationale: Although framed broadly around multiple uses of water in the Kirindi Oya irrigation system, this empirical mixed-methods study directly investigates household and community domestic water service access (NWS&DB piped standposts, wells, and dry-season domestic canal releases) through household surveys, standpipe observations, focus groups, and interviews with NWS&DB and Standpipe Committees. It analyzes rule-type mechanisms under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope—permitted-use restrictions, monthly standpost tariffs (Rs 11), collective enforcement via disconnection and Rs 250 reconnection fees, informal user accommodation/discretion for non-drinking domestic uses, drought priority rules, and institutional membership rules excluding domestic and female users—alongside empirical outcomes on domestic water access and standpipe supply reliability/intermittency. Eligible for systematic review inclusion (qualitative/mechanism synthesis).
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods empirical case study (stratified household survey, direct observations at standpipes and tanks, focus group discussions, water quality measurements, and key informant interviews)
